question: How much faster has the World Bank Group made project preparation and approval?

results.text:
• Greater efficiency

and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to
address our clients’ priorities. We cut average project-approval times from

We’re deploying AI to accelerate our work and working with partners to promote

applications that solve everyday problems in developing countries.
• Clear outcomes
Our Scorecard now focuses on 22 key metrics that show how our work creates
jobs and improves lives. And our Target Map keeps us ambitious against 10
strategic priorities. We publish our data online, making it more user-friendly and
leading to better outcomes.

question: What share of Jordan's domestic water supply is the Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project expected to deliver by 2030?

results.text:
The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected
to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply.
The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly,
approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation.
The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing
financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of
up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million
concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green
Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of
up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness.
The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments,
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water
security, economic growth, and job creation.

needed to secure power imports from the EU. Another project is rehabilitating

question: How many family farms does the World Bank Group partnership with Brazil aim to support by 2030, and with what kind of help?

results.text:
Brazil’s family farms employ nearly 10 million people and play a central
role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched
in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved
technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030.
This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority
that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus.
Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique
capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations
of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural
roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards,
repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally,
the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s
guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the
World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across
all three pillars.

With this approach, we’ll create an integrated pathway for family
farms to access markets, finance, technology, and resilience tools.
We’re working quickly because family farms around the world, including
500 million smallholder farmers, produce most of the world’s food,
yet many remain in poverty, relying on traditional farming methods
and lacking access to markets, finance, and technology. Supporting
them to become commercially successful is critical to creating jobs,
reducing poverty, and improving global food security. Our strategy
unlocks the knowledge, capital, and political will to seize that potential.

question: By how much has air passenger traffic in Cabo Verde grown since IFC began financing its airports?

results.text:
IFC has anchored the private sector transformation. In December 2023,
IFC arranged a financing package of up to €35.5 million for Oásis Atlântico,
one of the country’s leading hospitality operators. The investment supports
more than 700 direct jobs and 20,000 indirect jobs, and linkages with over
700 small suppliers and farmers. IFC has also extended two successive
sustainability-linked loans to Cabo Verde Airports S.A., a subsidiary of VINCI
Airports, with the most recent reaching up to €60 million in February 2026.
The financing has modernized and greened the country’s seven airports,
created over 2,000 direct jobs and 1,200 indirect jobs, and helped establish
35 new air routes — driving a 60 percent surge in passenger volumes
since 2022.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a
quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow
model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s
10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a
shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent
framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and
its potential unrealized.
The World Bank Group has worked across its private and public sector
arms to help Cabo Verde chart a more diversified and inclusive tourism
sector. Two World Bank operations — the Resilient Tourism and Blue
Economy Development Project and the Improving Connectivity and Urban
Infrastructure Project — are strengthening the sector’s governance and
institutional framework, while upgrading critical infrastructure, including
coastal and jetty facilities, maritime passenger terminals, heritage sites,
and public spaces.

question: How long does a Country Partnership Framework typically span?

results.text:
COUNTRY ENGAGEMENT
We are building a One World Bank Group client
coverage model that aligns public and private sector
solutions around jobs, growth, and private investment.
Our new approach is more efficient, outcome-focused,
and systematic in tapping private sector solutions
and will help countries tackle their development
challenges with greater speed, quality, and impact.
The centerpiece of this new approach is our
Country Partnership Framework (CPF) — the
key tool that guides our strategic engagement
with countries. CPFs typically span four to six
years, with a maximum duration of 10 years, to
align our support with a country’s development
goals and the World Bank Group Scorecard.

During the Spring Meetings in April 2026, the
World Bank Group launched the Small States
Strategy. Guided by select solutions underpinned
by the World Bank Group Jobs Framework, the Strategy
prioritizes interventions with the greatest potential
to support job creation and economic growth.
Support will be differentiated to reflect individual
country contexts, while using regional approaches,
aggregated procurement, capacity building, and
stronger partnerships to address scale constraints,
high transaction costs, and partner fragmentation.
Implementation is anchored in Country Partnership
Frameworks. The Strategy was informed by feedback
from small states gathered through consultations
and engagement, including at the annual Small States
Forum held alongside the World Bank Group Annual
Meetings in October 2025.
For more information, visit https://www.
worldbank.org/en/country/smallstates.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE

In fiscal 2026, we delivered 28 new CPFs that are
underpinned by five core diagnostics: Country
Climate and Development Reports, Country
Growth and Jobs Reports, Country Private Sector
Diagnostics, Poverty and Equity Assessments, and
Public Finance Reviews. From this data, we identify
three to five outcomes that support job creation,
and complementary public and private actions to
support the outcomes. With outcomes defined at the
intersection of three selectivity criteria — development
challenges, country development goals, and World
Bank Group comparative advantages — CPFs
serve as the primary vehicle for translating World
Bank Group targets and strategies into countrylevel action, delivering on client priorities through
complementary public and private solutions.

steadily pursued its stated mission for nearly four
decades by providing guarantees to private investors.
This paves the way for private funds to flow to emerging
and developing economies, enabling job creation.

ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL POLICIES
In fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group enhanced its
Environmental and Social (E&S) management
structure by integrating E&S teams from the World
Bank (IBRD/IDA), IFC, and MIGA at the corporate
level, establishing a global World Bank Group E&S
Policy and Operations department and a global World
Bank Group E&S Risk department. The new structure
provides a more robust system for proactive risk
management and helps us deliver safeguards with
greater clarity, speed, and credibility, while reinforcing
our commitment to quality and accountability.

question: What was MIGA's gross outstanding guarantee portfolio as of June 30, 2026?

results.text:
MIGA’s new guarantee business volume during
fiscal 2026 reached a record high of $10.6 billion in
support of 60 projects, compared to $9.5 billion
of new guarantees issued in fiscal 2025 in support of
44 projects. Due to record new business volume, as
of June 30, 2026, MIGA’s gross outstanding guarantee
portfolio reached a record high of $41.4 billion,
representing a 13 percent increase. The net outstanding
guarantee portfolio increased by 8 percent to a record
high of $12.1 billion.

MIGA ceded $7.5 billion of new business to the
reinsurance market during fiscal 2026. MIGA’s objective
in using reinsurance is to support its growth while
managing portfolio concentration and ensuring
efficient capital utilization. The increased use of
reinsurance is also in line with the World Bank Group
goal of leveraging the private sector into financing
development, as well as with MIGA’s strategy of
preserving capital to fund future growth, primarily
in priority areas. As of June 30, 2026, $28.7 billion or
69 percent of the outstanding gross portfolio was
reinsured, up from 68 percent last fiscal year.

The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), home of the World Bank Group Guarantee
Platform, provides guarantees to facilitate the flow of foreign investment in developing countries,
enabling the private sector to create jobs. Our mandate is to encourage investment into developing
member countries by providing non-commercial risk guarantees (political risk insurance, credit
enhancement products, and trade finance guarantees) to investors and lenders.
In fiscal 2026, MIGA marked a major milestone by
surpassing $100 billion in cumulative guarantees
issued since its founding in 1988. With just $366 million
of paid-in capital from member countries, MIGA has
steadily pursued its stated mission for nearly four
decades by providing guarantees to private investors.
This paves the way for private funds to flow to emerging
and developing economies, enabling job creation.

question: How much did the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform issue in guarantees in fiscal 2026, and to how many projects?

results.text:
In its second year, fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group
Guarantee Platform issued $17.9 billion in guarantees
to 110 projects in 32 countries, an increase of
46 percent over fiscal 2025. Of this, MIGA issued a
record $10.6 billion in new guarantees across 60
projects. Through these projects, MIGA encouraged
private investment to facilitate economic development
in host countries by helping clients manage and
mitigate non-commercial risks. The majority of projects
advanced at least one of MIGA’s strategic priorities: 38
projects were climate finance initiatives, 20 projects
were in IDA–eligible countries, and 10 projects were in
fragile and conflict-affected situations.
As a result, the fiscal 2026 issuances are expected to:
• Mobilize $11 billion in private capital
• Provide 300,000 people and businesses with
access to finance
• Strengthen food and nutrition security for
4 million people
• Enable 2.7 gigawatts in renewable energy capacity

This more than
threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in
our ability to bring external capital into development
opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer
of private capital among multilateral development
banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group
Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal
2026. We are providing patient equity in markets
where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding
local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk
would otherwise deter investment. We also began
piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect
institutional investors with emerging market assets at
greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings
agencies with historical data on the performance
of emerging market lending through the Global
Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical
shifts are already supporting investment and jobs.
A NEW APPROACH TO

The World Bank Group Guarantee Platform,
hosted at MIGA, continues to play a vital role in
bringing private capital to emerging markets.
The Board commends MIGA for surpassing
$100 billion in cumulative guarantee issuance
since its founding in 1988, a remarkable
achievement from just $366 million in paid-in
capital. In addition, in fiscal 2026, the World Bank
Group surpassed its goal of $20 billion in annual
guarantee issuance — four years ahead of the
2030 target.
The Board endorsed the extension of the World
Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan, a
significant step that provides vital continuity for
countries. The Executive Directors expect the
institution to be measured by the tangible impact
its work has on communities worldwide, and the
Board is grateful for the strong collaboration with
Management on this initiative.

question: As of June 2026, how many countries had implemented at least one instrument from the Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit?

results.text:
This approach facilitates both vertical programs,
which involve in-depth, sustained engagement within
a single country, and horizontal programs, which
encompass multiple countries, states within a country,
or subnational entities. In fiscal 2026, the World Bank
approved 33 new programs totaling $25.1 billion in
financing, comprising 15 vertical programs ($8.2 billion)
and 18 horizontal programs ($16.9 billion). Total MPA
project approvals comprised 95 projects totaling
$17.7 billion, including nine additional financing
projects totaling $1.0 billion.
As of June 2026, a total of 80 countries have
implemented at least one instrument from the Crisis
Preparedness and Response Toolkit. With those
instruments, countries have pre-arranged contingent
resources and catastrophe bonds/insurance, allowing
them to focus on disaster recovery.

Fiscal 2026 marked the start of the IDA21 policy
package, which took effect on July 1, 2025, with support
from 57 donors. As it supports IDA countries to chart
their own paths toward sustainable development,
IDA21 will benefit more than 1.9 billion people
worldwide and sustain IDA’s strong track record of
innovation and results.
IDA also collaborated with think tanks and foundations
on the IDA20 retrospective report and engaged civil
society organizations in donor countries on its lessons.
In fiscal 2026, 78 countries were eligible for IDA
support.7 New IDA lending commitments for fiscal
2026 totaled $30.8 billion for 237 operations, of
which 13 were IBRD/IDA blended operations. These
commitments included $22.1 billion in credits,
$0.8 billion in guarantees, and $7.9 billion in grants.
In addition, 37 projects totaling $564 million were
approved for support from the IDA21 IDA-IFC-MIGA
Private Sector Window (PSW) during the fiscal year.

The Executive Directors support the World Bank
Group’s urgent response to these crises while
maintaining a resolute focus on the long-term
challenge of creating jobs at scale. The Board is
encouraged that countries can increasingly access
fast-acting finance for emergency response,
with 79 countries to date utilizing Crisis Toolkit
Arrangements. In fiscal 2026, the Board reaffirmed
its support for the World Bank Group’s strategic
drive to create more and better-paid jobs as total
World Bank Group commitments for the year
reached $123.5 billion.1
The Board welcomes the World Bank Group’s
new ways of working. By deepening collaboration
across our institutions, we are enhancing
efficiency and accelerating our impact on the
ground. Forging new alliances with private
sector partners and clients and strengthening
cooperation with development partners ensures
that scarce resources are deployed where they can
generate the most jobs and growth.

question: What was IFC's net income in fiscal 2026?

results.text:
Over the past several years, IFC has been shifting
its model to not only deploy its own capital but to
mobilize more private capital from partners. That
shift is reflected in our fiscal 2026 results. The World
Bank Group mobilized $112 billion in private capital
in fiscal 2026, more than tripling from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022. IFC contributes to that outcome through
a range of instruments and products — guarantees,
originate-to-distribute structures, catalytic equity,
syndications, anchor investments, transaction
advisory, and local-currency financing — each designed
to address specific barriers that have historically
constrained private investment in developing
economies. In fiscal 2026, IFC achieved a record
$105.6 billion in investment commitments, including
over $73.6 billion in private capital mobilized.
Those investments translate into real-world outcomes
for millions of people. The expected impact of IFC’s
portfolio in fiscal 2026 includes:

IFC’s green and social bonds are an integral part of its
borrowing strategy with $2 billion and $4 billion issued
in fiscal 2026, respectively. In January 2026, IFC issued
a three-year $2 billion social bond with proceeds
funding a diverse range of social projects which include
affordable basic infrastructure (e.g., clean drinking
water, energy, transport); access to essential services;
food security and affordable housing; and womenowned small- and medium-sized businesses, among
other sectors. Read more in IFC’s Green and Social Bond
Annual Impact Report.
FINANCIAL INNOVATIONS TO

We also assess and track the development impact
of the advisory services that we provide to our
clients to help them adopt modern technologies
and management practices in various areas. In fiscal
2026, 60 percent of our completed advisory projects
implemented with client companies were found to
be mostly successful or better, below IFC’s target of
65 percent and the success rate in fiscal 2025. The
decline is driven primarily by project-specific design
and implementation issues, deliberate portfolio
clean-up efforts, and external disruptions that were
largely outside project control and created significant
implementation challenges across multiple business
lines and geographies.
